stories.headline: Colombia declares an emergency after a 7.4-magnitude earthquake kills at least 130

sources.body:
At least 132 people are dead and a state of emergency has been declared after Colombia was hit by one of its largest earthquakes in years.

The death toll is likely to rise, with more feared trapped under collapsed buildings.

The magnitude 7.4 quake struck at 07:34 (12:34 GMT) at a depth of 103km (64 miles) in Chocó province, the country's geological service said. It was felt across an enormous area, stretching for hundreds of miles across western Colombia.

Many of the deaths have been concentrated in the city of Pereira, in Colombia's coffee-growing region, with surrounding cities and the Valle del Cauca region also hit hard.

The epicentre of the quake was near the village of San José del Palmar, in Chocó province, but local mayor León Fabio Marín Moncada said that there had miraculously been no deaths or injuries - despite the roads in and out being damaged.

More than 480 people were injured in the quakes, Colombia's Association of Capital Cities wrote in a statement update on Monday.

About 55km (34 miles) from the epicenter of the earthquake, the city of Pereira saw some of the worst damage.

Videos verified by the BBC show at least one building collapsing in Plaza Bolívar, the city's main square, with scattered debris and dust across the open space where many people had gathered.

Local authorities have reported at least 40 people dead in the city's metropolitan area, with 65 collapsed buildings. People are believed to be trapped in 15 of them.

A curfew is in place in some parts of the city until 05:00 local time on Tuesday.

Thirty-two buildings collapsed in Cali, located about 160km south of Pereira and about 200km from the epicentre.

Dan Cutler, 29, is from London but has been in Colombia for about two months as part of a big trip with his partner, and is currently in Cali.

Being woken by the earthquake, he told the BBC: "I've never experienced anything like it."

"We sprinted outside in our pyjamas. There's no major structural damage to the hotel, but there are surface cracks in the walls, and paint and plaster have peeled off," he says.

There were also reports of deaths in Manizales, Quibdó, Medellín, across the Chocó and Valle del Cauca regions.

At least two people have died in Manizales.

Speaking to BBC World Service, Angélica Ávila said she had been staying in a hotel in Manizales.

She said as the earthquake hit, cracks appeared in the walls.

"Everyone was screaming... I saw dust coming out of the neighbouring buildings, and bricks were falling off the walls," she said.

Journalist and meteorologist Luis Felipe Molina, from Manizales, was at home when the earthquake struck - about 150km from the epicentre.

He explained that due to previous earthquakes, the city has "very strict seismic-resistant building regulations" - so his building was able to resist the impact.

"I have 450 books and only a few were left standing on the shelves. You could hear glass breaking and people screaming," he told BBC Mundo.

"It was a terrible and terrifying experience."

The country's aviation authority has reported damage at several regional airports, including those in Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura.
sources.headline: At least 132 killed in Colombia's largest earthquake in years

sources.body:
Quake of 7.4 magnitude collapses and severely damages buildings in several major cities, including Cali and Pereira

More than 100 people died after a powerful earthquake struck western Colombia , collapsing and severely damaging scores of buildings in major cities including Cali and Pereira.

The US and Colombian geological surveys reported that a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck at 7.34am local time on Monday, with its epicentre in the western department of Chocó. It was felt in neighbouring Venezuela, still reeling from a deadly double earthquake on 24 June.

Colombia’s president, Abelardo de la Espriella, said 111 people had been killed and 87 injured, while 61 buildings had collapsed.

“The ⁠national government has all of its capabilities deployed to protect lives, assist affected communities and deliver aid wherever it is ​needed,” he said in a national address at about 1pm local time upon declaring ‌a national state of emergency. “The first priority is rescuing the people trapped under the rubble.”

Western Colombia appeared to have suffered the most serious damage. Authorities reported 27 deaths in the Valle del Cauca department, 40 deaths in Pereira, the capital of Risaralda department, and at least two in Manizales, the capital of Caldas.

The mayor of Manizales, Jorge Eduardo Rojas Giraldo, said at least 12 buildings and 20 homes had been partially or completely or destroyed.

In a video post, he told citizens to be “completely ready” for aftershocks. “Do not go back into the buildings yet. I know this isn’t easy but stay outside for a little while at least because there could be an aftershock.”

Social media videos showed people searching for victims in the wreckage of a four-storey hotel in Cali and a woman sprinting from a building as it collapsed in Manizales.

One video showed part of San José church in Pereira collapsing as palm trees around it shook. Another video published by the newspaper El Tiempo captured the moment a building gave way in Manizales.

The mayor of Cali, Alejandro Eder, said at least 20 buildings collapsed in his city and people were trapped inside.

“Right now, we are trying to map out what has happened, firstly to protect lives and secondly to be able to push ahead with any kind of rescue that might be necessary,” he said, urging citizens to stay calm.

He told residents to check their buildings for structural damage. “If you do not feel safe, if you see very large cracks, please leave the building.”

In an interview, the mayor of Pereira, Mauricio Salazar, said 65 buildings had collapsed, with victims thought to be trapped in at least 15 of them. Five of the city’s hospitals were reportedly inundated with the injured.

Raúl Andrés Buitrago, the head of customer service at a business in Pereira, said he was leaving for work when the seismic alert on his watch went off.

“There are often little tremors here,” he said. “But I’d never felt an earthquake like this. It started softly, softly, softly, then it felt like it was getting stronger every second.”
sources.headline: Scores dead in Colombia after powerful earthquake strikes west of country

sources.body:
Urgent search for survivors in Colombia after strongest quake of the century brings down buildings in western provinces.

Al Jazeera reporter on the ground as Colombia quake death toll rises

At least 132 people have been killed and hundreds remain missing after a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck Colombia, the most powerful tremor to hit the country this century, according to the Colombian Geological Service.

The quake on Monday ravaged cities across western Colombia, including Cali, Pereira, Quibdo and Manizales, and was felt in neighbouring Ecuador and Panama.

The epicentre was in San Jose Del Palmar in the Choco region, about 400km (250 miles) west of the capital, Bogota, the US Geological Survey said. The quake struck at a depth of 107km (66 miles).

At least 21 aftershocks followed within hours.

In Cali, the country’s third-largest city, search teams and civilians picked through the remains of destroyed buildings, passing large pieces of concrete and other rubble down a long line of volunteers. Local officials said at least 20 buildings crumbled, while 380 were damaged, trapping many people.

Jorge Moncayo, a 64-year-old taxi driver in Cali, told The Associated Press news agency that he saw plumes of dust shoot up across the city as buildings collapsed.

“My entire house shook. I’ve never lived through such a powerful earthquake,” he said. “We’re thanking God we’re alive.”

Juan Carlos Osorio told Caracol Television that the collapse of one building “sounded like a bomb”, as he helped remove debris from a collapsed structure in Cali.

“All of us neighbours are working together, forming human chains. We ⁠need heavy equipment. There are many people trapped.”

The earthquake struck just days after Abelardo de La Espriella was sworn in as president , thrusting the new administration into its first major crisis, with memories still fresh of devastating twin earthquakes in neighbouring Venezuela in June.

“The national government has all of its capabilities deployed to protect lives, ⁠assist affected communities and deliver aid wherever it is needed,” he said in a national address at about 1pm local time (18:00 GMT), upon declaring a national state of emergency.

“The first priority is rescuing the people trapped under the rubble.”

De La Espriella said preliminary reports indicated 111 dead and 87 injured, along with dozens of collapsed buildings and damaged homes. The Colombian Association of Capital Cities, a think tank, said at least 132 people were killed and 570 others injured.

Local authorities said the death toll included at least 40 people killed in the Risaralda region, part of Colombia’s coffee-growing area. Pereira, the region’s capital, suffered extensive damage, with rescue workers continuing to search collapsed buildings for survivors.

At least 27 people died in the Valle del Cauca region, where Cali is located, including three children.

Reports from Choco, near the epicentre, were slowed by communications outages, with some areas still lacking mobile phone service hours after the earthquake. Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said 12 people had been killed and 84 injured in the largely rural area.
sources.headline: Colombia declares emergency after 7.4 magnitude earthquake kills 130

stories.headline: Trump demands compensation from Iran as talks continue over the Strait of Hormuz

sources.body:
US president’s statement is latest sign that negotations to end war and reopen strait of Hormuz have stalled

Donald Trump has said he will demand that Iran pay compensation for the deaths of thousands of US soldiers and Iran’s own civilians killed in recent decades in the latest sign his negotiations to end the war and reopen the strait of Hormuz have reached an impasse.

The US president is trying to end conflicts in Iran , Gaza and Lebanon, and his additional demands of Iran are likely to provoke anger in Tehran at the same time as Israel has rejected Trump’s terms for a 15-point roadmap to end the war in Gaza.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump said he was issuing the demand for war reparations in response to Iranian negotiators making similar claims for damages for the five-month war that has killed thousands and devastated Iran’s military and economy.

“Now I am likewise demanding compensation from Iran, for all of the people that they have killed and gravely wounded with their roadside bombs and many conflicts, for which they are famous, as led initially by Gen Soleimani, including the families of those killed on the USS Cole, and thousands of others killed in combat,” he wrote on Truth Social.

“Additionally, compensation should be paid to the families of the hundreds of thousands of innocent protesters that Iran has killed over the last 50 years, not to mention the 52,000 that have been killed in the last five months.”

The demands are likely to be a nonstarter for Iran’s leaders in the careful peace negotiations aimed at reopening the strait of Hormuz, through which 20% of global oil trade flowed before the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in late February. Trump and other senior negotiators have claimed many times that a deal is imminent, although none has materialised.

The remarks followed a series of setbacks for Trump’s efforts to end several Middle East conflicts before the midterm elections in November, in which high oil prices and inflation will probably hurt fellow Republicans at the polls.

On Sunday, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said he rejected the Trump-backed Board of Peace’s 15-point plan to end Israel’s war in Gaza . Netanyahu had said Hamas must fully disarm before Israel would consider pulling out of Gaza, rather than the phased withdrawal proposed by the Board of Peace.

Netanyahu framed the decision as a rejection of US pressure on Israel to make peace in several wars in the Middle East. “Unlike all those who lecture us, we do what needs to be done for Israel’s security, and we can and know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary,” Netanyahu said.

Trump has not replied to Netanyahu’s statement, which was a remarkably public break between the leaders of the US and its closest ally in the Middle East. But in response to a shouted question in the Oval Office on Monday, he said his relationship with Netanyahu was “very good”.

Trump has sought to increase pressure on Iran. An hour after his first post demanding war reparations from Tehran, he broadened their scope to include the victims of recent wars throughout the region.
sources.headline: Trump demands Iran pay compensation for decades of US soldier deaths

sources.body:
US president seeks payment for ’50 years’ of alleged damages after Iran conditions reopening of Hormuz on war reparations.

Trump to demand compensation for Tehran’s ‘conflicts’

United States President Donald Trump has demanded compensation from Iran for those he claimed were killed by the country after Tehran conditioned the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz on receiving war reparations from Washington.

Trump told reporters at the White House on Monday that his administration was going to seek payment for “50 years” of damages caused by Iran, framing the move as a direct response to Tehran’s claims.

Tehran has said it will not open the Strait of Hormuz – through which about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas flowed before the US-Israel war on Iran – unless Washington agrees to pay war reparations and end sanctions. The Iranian demands were largely in line with the terms of an interim peace agreement signed in June, which has since broken down over a dispute on control over the strait.

Talks between Iran and Oman over the waterway, which separates the two countries, are ongoing, but Trump’s new demands risk complicating efforts to reopen the maritime passage.

“They asked for reparations, you might say. Or they asked for money for the damage that we’ve done. I said that’s a good idea,” he told reporters. “Well, we’re going to ask for money for the damage they’ve done over a 50-year period.”

The payments would cover deaths among US forces in the region as well as civilian protesters in Iran, he said, claiming that 52,000 people have been killed in Iran in the past four months. Tehran says some 3,117 people died in antigovernment protests that swept the country in January, prior to the launch of the US-Israel war.

The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) in February reported about 7,000 deaths, including 6,500 protesters.

Trump also said Tehran should compensate families of the 17 US sailors killed in an October 2000 attack in Yemen on the USS Cole naval vessel, which has been blamed on al-Qaeda, not Iran.

“Also, with respect to the Iran negotiations, Iran should be responsible for the damages and death caused to the people of Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and Gaza!” he wrote in a Truth Social post.

Since the US-Israel war on Iran began on February 28, Trump has repeatedly oscillated between threats of escalation and claims that a peace deal is imminent.

He threatened last week to “hit” Iran “very hard”, only to pull back, hinting a peace deal was near. This weekend, he said he was “low-keying” his approach to the conflict, suggesting that he was prepared to let economic pressure mount in place of further military strikes.

Charles Kupchan, a former special assistant to ex-US President Barack Obama, described Trump’s remarks about requiring compensation as “banter” and said both sides have strong incentives to reach a deal.

“Unfortunately, we are just looking at some back-and-forth banter here, where neither the Iranians nor the Trump administration is being serious,” he told Al Jazeera.
sources.headline: Trump demands compensation from Iran as talks on Strait of Hormuz continue

stories.headline: Netanyahu rejects Trump’s Gaza plan, saying Israel will not withdraw until Hamas disarms

sources.body:
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may have categorically rejected the new Board of Peace roadmap to disarm Hamas in Gaza, but that is unlikely to be the final word.

The White House is reportedly "not bothered" by Netanyahu's statement and views it as campaign rhetoric in the run-up to a heated general election.

"We understand Bibi's political needs" the Israeli journalist, Barak Ravid, quotes a senior US official as saying – using a nickname to refer to the Israeli leader. "We have no problem with it as long as he continues to do what we ask – especially regarding restraining attacks in Gaza."

Recent days have seen an apparent pause in Israel's strikes on Gaza – something Hamas had demanded when signing on to the US-backed, 15-point roadmap .

And there is another suggestion that Israel is ready to advance US President Donald Trump's peace plan for Gaza – getting ready for the deployment of the International Stabilization Force (ISF). The force is made up of international troops, with the plan being for them to work with a new Palestinian police force to secure the territory.

The expected construction of the first ISF base is still scheduled to begin amid the ruins of Rafah in southern Gaza at the end of this month, according to Israeli public radio, Kan News, which would allow reconstruction to begin at last.

In July, after months of delicate negotiations, Trump announced a "major milestone" in the implementation of his plan to end Israel's war in Gaza.

Writing on his Truth Social platform, Trump said that the Board of Peace had reached an agreement for the complete disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups in the territory.

The deal is meant to be carried out in phases, with all weapons decommissioned and stored by a new Palestinian administration in Gaza – which reports to the Board of Peace - and Israeli forces withdrawing from the more than 60% of Gaza they currently control.

Senior Hamas officials confirmed that they had agreed to the new framework, conditioning it on mutual compliance by Israel. This was widely viewed as a major potential breakthrough in the conflict. The UK welcomed it and the European Union hailed it as a "crucial step".

However, for more than a week, Israel did not give its formal response.

An Israeli spokesman said only that the roadmap did not "reflect Israel's positions." A far-right member of the government, Itamar Ben-Gvir, wrote on X that the deal was "unacceptable."

Increasingly, mainstream Israeli opposition politicians also raised doubts. They questioned whether all small arms would be decommissioned and the sequencing of the plan.

Finally on Sunday, Netanyahu told his cabinet, "I wish to be precise here: Israel does not accept the 15-point document."

He added: "The IDF [Israel Defense Forces] will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed. And when I say the disarming of Hamas, it means heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry. And we are talking about genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament."
sources.headline: Netanyahu's rejection of Trump's 15-point Gaza plan unlikely to be final word

sources.body:
Israeli prime minister faces incompatible demands from his far-right government ministers and from Donald Trump

Benjamin Netanyahu’s public rejection of a US-backed deal for Gaza drew scepticism in Israel, amid reports he was personally hammering out details of a pilot military withdrawal days earlier.

The Israeli prime minister is struggling to balance incompatible demands on Gaza policy from his key domestic and international allies.

The far-right Israeli politicians who prop up Netanyahu’s coalition government want to intensify Israeli attacks on Gaza and establish settlements inside the territory.

Donald Trump, who provides vital diplomatic and military backing for Israel, wants to move toward a permanent settlement and return to Palestinian control in Gaza, brokered by the Board of Peace that he created and chairs.

With an Israeli election looming in just over two months, Netanyahu appears to have opted to publicly placate domestic partners who are already on the campaign trail.

On Sunday, he rejected a new 15-point plan for Gaza, which included a Hamas commitment to give up its weapons, meeting a key Israeli demand. He also resisted US pressure to end wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran without Israel’s buy-in.

The remarks blindsided Israeli commanders, who had been discussing the implementation of the plan in meetings with Netanyahu and the IDF’s chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, days earlier, Israel’s Channel 12 television reported.

“We learned about it today from the media,” the station quoted a defence official as saying. “At the meetings that were held until now, the prime minister personally gave his consent to this plan and to a withdrawal from the points in Rafah.”

The meetings covered precise boundaries of three pilot areas in southern Gaza where a proposed international force – which has yet to be stood up – could take over from the Israeli military, and the interface between the two forces, the report said.

Netanyahu’s public attack on the Board of Peace plan seemed like a particularly pointed rejection of US goals because it was released soon after a reported visit by Adm Brad Cooper, who heads US Central Command.

He came to deliver in person the message that the Trump administration wants Israel to end its wars in Gaza and Lebanon, Israeli media reported. “The Americans’ message to the IDF was to move in the direction of shutting down all three theatres of operations,” a senior Israeli military officer told Channel 13 Television.

Defying Trump, who is notoriously thin-skinned and intolerant of dissent, is risky when Israel is internationally isolated and needs US military supplies.

But Netanyahu has a long track record of audacious political manoeuvring, both at home and internationally, undaunted even by ostensible power imbalances. Bill Clinton, after meeting him for the first time in 1996, is reported to have said: “Who’s the fucking superpower here?”

In May 2024, the then US president, Joe Biden, announced an Israeli-backed ceasefire and hostage release plan for Gaza, only to have Netanyahu distance himself from the proposal and ultimately reject it.
sources.headline: Flip-flopping Netanyahu rejects Gaza plan but cannot placate all his allies

sources.body: Benjamin Netanyahu said Sunday that Israel’s military “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed.” The White House has not commented on the Israeli Prime Minister’s dismissal of Trump’s deal for Gaza.
sources.headline: Netanyahu says no Gaza withdrawal until Hamas disarms

stories.headline: Ukrainian drone strike deep inside Russia kills at least 13

sources.body:
At least 13 people have been killed in a Ukrainian drone strike on the Russian republic of Tatarstan, local officials have said.

They confirmed one child was among those killed, with 75 more people injured as drones hit Nizhnekamsk, more than 1,100 kilometres (680m) from the Ukrainian border. Ukraine's Armed Forces said the city's Tanevo oil refinery had been hit.

It is one of the deadliest single attacks on Russia since the start of Moscow's full-scale war in Ukraine in 2022.

Kyiv has recently stepped up its long-range strikes on facilities it says contribute revenue and logistics to Russia's war on Ukraine.

The strike on Nizhnekamsk lasted several hours overnight and into the morning, according to local sources.

Verified images on social media show large plumes of smoke and flames rising into the sky in daytime, with air raid sirens howling in the background.

The Uzkbek consulate in Tatarstan said seven of those killed were citizens of Uzbekistan.

According to Russian news agency RIA, most of the victims had been staying in a hostel at the time of the attack, and Russia's Investigative Committee said that "civilian individuals who were not involved in any military operations were present" where the drones struck.

The BBC has not independently verified this information. Moscow said that "all those involved in the attacks" would "face inevitable and severe punishment".

Oil refineries in Nizhnekamsk had already been hit once - on 12 June.

"The facilities Ukraine targets are used to carry out attacks against Ukraine, manufacture weapons, support Russia's war effort," said Andriy Kovalenko, head of the Ukraine's Centre for Countering Disinformation.

The head of Tatarstan, Rustam Minnikhanov, confirmed the strike and shared his condolences with the families of the deceased, while Nizhnekamsk Mayor Radmir Belayev said the deaths had been a "a tremendous pain for all of us".

Ukraine's Kovalenko said "every civilian death in Russia is on [President Vladimir] Putin" and that "Russians should direct their grievances at Putin and at the decisions made within their own country".

"Without Putin, there would have been no aggression. Without the aggression, these people would still be alive," he added.

More than 450 Ukrainian drones were shot down by the Russian air defences overnight across Russia, Moscow said.

Elsewhere in Russia, fires broke out when an industrial facility in Siberia's Tyumen region was hit by several falling drones, according to local authorities.

Kyiv has become increasingly successful at carrying out long-range strikes on Russia, often targeting warehouses or energy infrastructure, with civilian casualties mounting.

Moscow, meanwhile, continues to target Ukraine with regular large-scale aerial attacks on cities and residential centres. Last week, a combined drone and missile strike on Kyiv killed 21 people.
sources.headline: At least 13 killed in Ukrainian drone strike deep into Russia

sources.body:
Attack hundreds of miles from border would be among deadliest of war as Kyiv aims to strangle Russian economy

A Ukrainian drone strike on an industrial city deep inside Russia has killed at least 13 people, according to the local mayor, as Kyiv steps up its campaign of long-range strikes on targets far from the frontline.

Kyiv said it hit the Taneco refinery in the city of Nizhnekamsk, about 750 miles (1,200km) from the Ukrainian border. Footage circulating online appeared to show smoke rising from the refinery.

Ukraine’s general staff said the raid was part of a campaign to reduce the “military potential of the Russian aggressor”.

Russian investigators claimed civilian and industrial sites in the city had been hit. The head of the Tatarstan region, Rustam Minnikhanov, said a Ukrainian drone hit a hostel, killing nine people. He posted images showing a badly damaged building.

If the death toll is confirmed, the strike would be among the deadliest Ukrainian attacks on Russian territory since the full-scale invasion began in 2022, underscoring the growing reach of Kyiv’s strikes deep inside Russia.

The Uzbek consulate said in a Telegram post that seven of the victims were Uzbek citizens. Minnikhanov declared a day of mourning and Russian prosecutors opened a criminal case into alleged terrorism.

Local video footage showed Ukrainian drones buzzing above the city’s skyline, flying low over grey and box-like Soviet-era apartment blocks. Two plumes of black smoke could be seen rising above an industrial zone on the wooded outskirts of Nizhnekamsk.

The site is home to Taneco, one of Russia’s biggest and most technologically advanced oil refineries, owned by Tatneft. It also houses a plant that produces rubber and petrochemical products. Ukraine also bombed the area in June.

In an address on Sunday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said “long-range sanctions” against the Kremlin and its war machine would continue. In recent months Ukrainian drones have wreaked havoc on Russia’s oil export industry, even hitting refineries in Siberia, 1,500 miles from the frontline.

The governor of the Tyumen region in western Siberia said on Monday that several Ukrainian drones had fallen on an industrial facility and that emergency services were dealing with a fire.

There have been several strikes on warehouses belonging to Wildberries, Russia’s equivalent of Amazon, as well as on oil tankers in the Sea of Azov and Black Sea. Ukraine’s long-term goal is to slowly strangle the Russian economy so Moscow can no longer fund its war.

Zelenskyy described his country’s remote bombing campaign as “entirely justified”. “Every Russian strike [on Ukrainian towns and cities] will be met with our response. Russia’s war will be felt more and more at their own home – in Russia,” he said on social media. “The only reason this is still continuing is Russia’s unwillingness to end this war.”

Russia’s defence ministry said it had intercepted 456 Ukrainian drones flying above Russian territory and annexed Crimea. Ukraine says it is knocking out its opponent’s air defence systems more quickly than they can be replaced, creating air corridors or “doors” it can exploit.
sources.headline: Ukraine drone strike on oil refinery deep inside Russia kills at least 13

sources.body:
A day of mourning has been declared in the Russian republic of Tatarstan after a Ukrainian drone attack killed 13 people.

At least 13 people, including a child, have been killed in a Ukrainian drone attack on the Russian city of Nizhnekamsk, authorities said, as Ukraine’s military said it targeted an oil facility in the region.

Monday’s attack in the Tatarstan region, about 800km (497 miles) east of Moscow, wounded at least 39 others, regional authorities said.

Regional head Rustam Minnikhanov denounced the attack as “barbaric” and said civilian infrastructure had been struck in a post on Telegram.

The Uzbek consulate in Kazan announced that at least seven of the 13 people killed were Uzbek citizens.

Between two and three million citizens of Uzbekistan, Central Asia’s most populous country, work in Russia, with the Uzbek economy partly based on remittances from migrants.

Uzbekistan has struck a diplomatic balance amid Russia’s war on Ukraine, maintaining close ties with Moscow while also stressing support for Kyiv’s territorial integrity.

The Russian defence ministry says it intercepted more than 450 Ukrainian drones overnight, as both sides continue to exchange heavy attacks.

Nizhnekamsk plays a crucial role in Russia’s oil exports, hosting one of the country’s largest and most advanced refineries. Ukraine’s military says it successfully struck the site in an overnight attack .

Svetlana Petrenko, spokesperson for the Investigative Committee of Russia, said a child was among the dead. Petrenko added that Kyiv had struck industrial facilities and civilians “who had no connection” to the country’s military. Russia has launched a criminal investigation into the strike, which it has called a “terrorist attack”.

“A criminal case has been opened regarding the terrorist attack carried out by Ukrainian armed forces on industrial and civilian facilities in the Republic of Tatarstan,” Petrenko told reporters on Monday.

Reporting from Moscow, Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova said “a day of mourning” had been declared in Tatarstan.

“This attack follows several similar attacks on the exact same industrial zone in June and July this year,” Shapovalova said.

“Ukraine’s constant long-range drone attacks on Russian regions are designed to dismantle the country’s war economy by crippling its fuel production, disrupting military logistics and exposing gaps in domestic air defences. Today, Ukraine has carried out one of its largest coordinated long-range strikes to date.”

Meanwhile, Major Robert “Magyar” Brovdi, the commander leading Ukraine’s drone war, said his country’s recent strikes in Crimea mark the first phase of a campaign aimed at rendering the peninsula unusable as a staging ground for Russian forces.

In an interview with AP, Brovdi said his forces were equipped at just 14 percent of what they would need to carry out the campaign at full capacity, adding that his forces would be able to strike seven times more targets if funds pledged by Western allies came quicker.

“Crimea falls within the key conceptual pillars on the path to ending the war,” he said.
sources.headline: At least 13 killed in Ukrainian drone attack on Russia’s Nizhnekamsk

stories.headline: WHO warns Ebola outbreak in DR Congo began months before its official emergency declaration

sources.body:
The latest Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo began at least three months before it was officially declared - meaning the health authorities are still playing catch-up, the World Health Organization (WHO) has warned.

More than 1,900 people have died from the virus since that declaration on 15 May, making this the second-worst Ebola outbreak ever.

Infection rates are still high, adding to the concern that the authorities are struggling to get to grips with the spread of the disease.

The epicentre of this outbreak of the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, is in the east of DR Congo where insecurity has hampered control efforts.

There is also no approved vaccine or any recognised therapeutic drugs, making treating Bundibugyo harder.

"We are chasing the virus, the virus is ahead of us," WHO Africa director Dr Mohamed Janabi said at a news conference in the city of Bunia, which is at the heart of this outbreak.

He cited research showing that the virus started spreading in February and was initially misdiagnosed as malaria or typhoid.

Janabi also said that, in part because of insecurity, health workers are only reaching about 30% of the cases with the rest dying at home.

Traditional burial practices – where mourners touch the deceased's body - and a suspicion of health authorities in some communities have also made things difficult.

But there are now several dedicated treatment centres in the east of DR Congo and people are getting diagnosed much more quickly.

So far there have been 4,294 confirmed cases and 1,960 deaths, DR Congo's health ministry has said.

The largest recorded outbreak was in West Africa between 2014 and 2016 when 11,325 people died.

Go to BBCAfrica.com for more news from the African continent.

Follow us on Twitter @BBCAfrica , on Facebook at BBC Africa or on Instagram at bbcafrica
sources.headline: We are chasing Ebola virus - it is ahead of us, WHO warns

sources.body: The WHO says that sequencing shows that the fast moving Ebola outbreak in DR Congo started about 3 months before the emergency was officially declared in May. Also, its crunch week for Zambia as voters gear up for elections. And a Rwandan mine has become one of the US's main suppliers of tungsten, a metal critical to the defence industry.
sources.headline: Ebola started 3 months earlier than official declaration

stories.headline: Western Europe records its hottest June and July on record amid drought and wildfire risk

sources.body:
Drought and wildfires intensify across continent, while tropical storms bring heavy rain and disruption to east Asia

High pressure has dominated central and eastern Europe in early August, breaking temperature records across the region. Austria recorded a high of 41.2C (106.2F), while Slovakia reached 42.2C. Hungary hit a peak of 41.8C, surpassing a record set in 1905, while overnight temperatures remained above 28C in some areas, marking it as a tropical night.

The extreme temperatures have been driven by a heat dome beneath the high-pressure system, which traps warm air close to the surface.

The prolonged heat has dried out soil and vegetation, creating conditions conducive to the spread of wildfires. Fires have burned across Italy, France, Serbia and Bulgaria, damaging forests and forcing residents to evacuate.

Water levels in the Danube, which flows through much of the affected region, have fallen to an all-time low . The receding river has exposed archaeological remains and wartime wreckage , including woolly mammoth bones, second world war ships and remains associated with the Roman-era Constantine’s Bridge.

Low water levels have also affected energy production, reducing the efficiency of nuclear power plants in Slovakia and Serbia and forcing Hungary to shut down a plant because there was insufficient water for cooling.

Meanwhile, a buoy in the Mediterranean recorded a sea-surface temperature of 33C. If verified, it would be the highest recorded in the region.

In eastern Asia, Typhoon Dolphin made landfall in China on Sunday. The national observatory had issued a red alert for the storm – the highest level – for prolonged heavy rainfall , high wind speeds and extensive damage. Dolphin has since weakened to a tropical storm.

Japan is braced for Typhoon Chan-hom, just days after Dolphin swept through northern Okinawa and the Amami islands. Chan-hom is expected to make landfall near the coast of Tohoku between Tuesday and Wednesday, with up to 80mph (129km/h) gusts and an atmospheric pressure of 985 hPa.

A third system, Peilou, formed on Sunday in the western Pacific. Although it is not expected to make landfall in the Philippines , it is likely to strengthen the south-west monsoon, bringing further rain across the country. Other typhoons this year have intensified the monsoon, which has killed six people and displaced more than 380,000.

sources.body:
US President Donald Trump has signed an order that calls for fewer childhood vaccines and also recommends splitting the mumps, measles and rubella (MMR) shots.

"Decades ago, children received only a small fraction of the vaccines required today," Trump said. "In those times, people were much healthier and of course the high rates of autism now observed did not exist."

The president has long cast doubt on the safety of MMR vaccines, but multiple studies have found no connection between the shots and autism.

The order also recommends that the number of childhood vaccines drop to 11 from the existing 18 recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP).

Trump's order serves as guidance, not a mandate, since shots required for school attendance are set at the state level, rather than by the federal government.

Speaking in the Oval Office on Monday, the president said his administration "is recognising gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations for only 11 core vaccinations against the most serious and dangerous diseases".

The immunisations recommended for all children under the order are for measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type B, pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus, and varicella or chicken pox.

"We're reducing them," Trump said. "It's not only that you're doing fewer vaccines, or jabs, as they say, but you're doing them in a series of visits to the doctor."

The president suggested the MMR vaccine could be "quite lethal" if given at once. He compared it to pouring a bottle of soda into a child's body.

When a reporter asked for evidence of the "lethal" claim, Trump said: "What I've heard is that there are some people that say it is that way."

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) , the MMR vaccine carries a very small risk of febrile seizures for young children. Those with health issues, including severe allegeric reactions or weakened immune systems, are advised to consult with healthcare providers before taking the shots.

The agency says "most people who get MMR vaccine do not have any serious problems with it", and that getting the vaccine "is much safer than getting measles, mumps, or rubella".

According to the CDC, there is "no published scientific evidence that shows any benefit in separating the combination MMR vaccine into three individual shots".

Experts say that allowing time between jabs means children are more likely to contract diseases in the interim or that they are more likely to miss appointments if there are multiple shots.

Trump's Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) Robert F Kennedy Jr said the proposed changes were meant to give parents choice, not prohibit access to childhood vaccines.

Since taking office in 2025, Kennedy has sought to change and loosen vaccine regulations. During a tense 20-minute interview on CNN last week, Kennedy insisted he had "never questioned the efficacy of the MMR vaccine".

Trump administration officials have said the order means children in the US would receive much less than the 72 shots recommended under the previous vaccine schedule, a figure that assumes annual flu and Covid-19 doses.

sources.body: KENOSHA, Wisconsin —   The progressive movement’s midterms march has arrived in Wisconsin, where a democratic socialist is forcing establishment Democrats to mount an all-out, last-ditch effort to stop her. State Rep. Francesca Hong is the front-runner to become the Democratic gubernatorial nominee, fueled by a populist campaign tapping into voters’ cost of living concerns. David Crowley, the Milwaukee County Executive backed by outgoing Gov. Tony Evers, has emerged as the top candidate trying to cut off Hong’s bid. Ahead of Tuesday’s primary, electability was top of mind for voters and both candidates as they raced to prove they could build the widest, strongest coalition against presumptive Republican nominee Tom Tiffany. Crowley and Evers have been barnstorming the swing state over the past week, warning a vote for Hong risks losing the governor’s mansion in November to Tiffany, a hard-right member of the House Freedom Caucus backed by President Donald Trump. “You know, it's the only time that I know that the governor — Tony Evers — the Republican Governors Association and Turning Point USA have ever been on the same page: in thinking that Francesca Hong is the best candidate to lose this race,” Crowley said in an interview at a local tavern in Sheboygan on Friday. Hong rejects those warnings. Speaking to voters at events across the state, Hong argues Democratic voters are fed up with the establishment ahead of November — and that she can appeal to a wide array of Democrats, Republicans and people who don’t feel represented by either party. “We have to take this moment, a movement moment, and be bold with transformative change, and build the actual big tent that we can and we must be as Democrats,” Hong told a crowd of about 50 people gathered at a senior community center in deep-red Siren. Hong, a 37-year-old former chef and single mother who represents the bluest district in the state assembly, has charted a remarkably rapid rise in a purple state that Trump won by just shy of 30,000 votes in 2024. She launched her campaign as a long shot, with far less name recognition than other Democrats in the race like Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez and former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes. Both of them have since dropped out . And despite being at a consistent fundraising disadvantage — Hong still has not put out a single television ad — the progressive has maintained wide leads in public polling. But Hong’s campaign has also faced intense scrutiny over a string of controversial past social media posts, including advocating for defunding the police and railing against Thanksgiving . She was later slammed for being unable to give a straightforward answer to CNN about whether she would “cancel Thanksgiving.” Following those missteps, Hong's team has clamped down on her interactions with both local and national media at campaign events in the final stretch. She has also moderated some of her past positions in public remarks, emphasizing repeatedly that she is “serious about public safety” and even attempting to eschew some of her anti-establishment ties. On Wednesday, she reversed herself on Thanksgiving, telling POLITICO that it was, in fact, her favorite holiday. And asked by POLITICO on Saturday if she had any regrets about her past, she told reporters at a campaign stop in Sheboygan that she had learned from her tweets. “I had some hot takes, some bad takes on Twitter, but when you're a business owner running a restaurant during Covid, trying to pay bills as a student, you're putting feelings out there into the world,” Hong said. “But I've evolved, I've learned. I think it's more dishonest not to learn.” Hong has leaned heavily into affordability policies, including raising the state’s minimum wage from $7.25 to $20, progressive taxation and a statewide one-year moratorium on data center construction — a salient issue in Wisconsin, where several local governments have already voted on moratoriums. “While many of our supporters or other folks have framed us as anti-establishment, what we are for is working-class people,” she told POLITICO. “It's not so much being anti-establishment as it is ensuring that we're listening to voters who are demanding change.” But many Democrats in the state worry her ideology — including the old social media posts hawking far-left talking points — will be a political risk in a battleground general election. Pro-Republican PACs, including one associated with the Republican Governors Association, have spent millions of dollars to boost Hong in the primary so they can face who they perceive to be a weaker candidate in November. Kyle Kilbourn, a Democrat who unsuccessfully ran against Tiffany for his House seat in 2024, said he still had not decided who to support in the primary because of concerns about “electability statewide.” “The last several elections have been very very close, by one or two percentage points, and so it matters,” he told POLITICO while attending a Hong event at a brewery in Rhinelander. Even some of Hong’s supporters are anxious. “It’s always going to be a concern,” Jan Stroman, who attended an event in River Falls, said when asked if Hong could win against Tiffany. Robert LaGesse, 74, said at an event in far-north Superior on Friday he was voting for Hong — but admitted Hong’s tweets about abolishing the police “sounds like a foolish statement that could hurt her big time.” At the same event, a young Hong campaign volunteer asked her about those social media posts. “I’m not going to abolish the police as governor,” Hong responded. “I cannot and I will not defund the police.” She was asked a similar version of the same question at nearly every other event last week. Some supporters also fear that Hong will face racist and sexist backlash as an Asian American woman. Wisconsin has never elected a governor who is not a white man. “There's a lot of sexism yet in our country,” Tim Freiss, 60 — a Hong supporter who previously voted for both Bush presidencies — said in an interview outside his home in Green Bay. “Honestly, what I'm worried about is her race, because our state is very racist,” another Hong supporter, Heidi Meyer, 48, said as Hong canvassed her neighborhood in Appleton. Democratic officials in the Badger State are determined to unify after the primary, but many are deeply concerned Hong isn’t running the disciplined campaign required to defeat a Trump-backed Republican in Wisconsin. The messy race has also deeply divided Democrats in the state. Hong’s allies bristle at Evers’ campaign against her, using his resources — including his own communications staff — to boost Crowley. Evers defeated Republican then-Gov. Scott Walker in 2018 by deploying his brand of more moderate Democratic policies to win over independents and limit deep losses in rural areas. But he decided not to run for a rare third term as governor. Evers on Friday would not commit to endorsing or campaigning with Hong should she win — though Democrats expect he’ll have to. “I want to have a chance to take a breath, and once that's in a position, we'll see,” Evers said in an interview as he walked with Crowley from a Hmong family-owned bakery in Sheboygan to the corner tavern packed with supporters. Crowley, asked if he would campaign for Hong this fall if she wins the nomination, shot back with a smile: “Ask her that too.” But he quickly added: “I want to be very clear: I'm not in this race running against any of my opponents. I'm running for the votes of Wisconsinites, and if they don't choose me to be the nominee, my job is to make sure that it's blue no matter who.” Asked Saturday if she would endorse and campaign with Crowley if he wins on Tuesday, Hong replied with one word: “Yes.” Hong has admitted the democratic socialist label comes with baggage — “I can't say I always love it for me,” she said at a restaurant in River Falls — but she also rejected the notion that her campaign is undisciplined and noted that establishment Democrats had consistently underestimated her bid. She hopes to work with Democrats across the ideological spectrum in the sprint toward November. “We’re a serious campaign that has built a movement and turned out new voters, folks who are voting for the first time,” Hong said. “We're a serious campaign that knows how to win, but we're also serious about working as a coalition and making sure that we collaborate and coordinate with the people that we need to to make sure we defeat Tom Tiffany in the fall.” Crowley has charted a more moderate path than Hong’s blistering democratic socialism. In an interview, he argued the party needs “someone who's not just going to fight back, but also who can sit at the negotiating table and be able to work with folks who want to deliver for those that we represent.” He also ruled out the data center moratorium popular with a wide swath of voters that Hong is running on and using to pull in some pockets of rural support: “So, the way I hear that question is that we're going to preempt local communities from not being able to focus on their own economic development,” Crowley said. There are signs that Crowley is making some gains. But he’s still 20 percentage points behind Hong in the latest polling . “Crowley is closing the gap, but it’s likely too little, too late,” said one longtime Wisconsin Democratic strategist, who was granted anonymity to candidly discuss the governor’s pick. Crowley’s team argues that Wisconsin polling is likely off just as it was in Michigan, where Abdul El-Sayed clinched the Democratic Senate nomination last week by a tighter than expected margin. But the signs of Hong’s strength are evident across the state, beyond just her stronghold of Madison. The first voter Crowley greeted at his opening Sheboygan stop Friday, Paige Gerber, said in an interview later she had already voted early for Hong. Supporters at the Crowley event later in the day were well aware of his standing. Voter after voter in interviews with POLITICO expressed alarm that their party was poised to pick Hong, a losing horse in their view. Retirees in “radicalized by basic decency” T-shirts sipped on beer and cheered when Evers walked through the door with Crowley, alongside local IBEW union workers and teachers. “Tony! Tony!” chants eventually rang through the bar. A Crowley staffer at one point tried to start a “David! David!” cheer. But it never caught on. Tyler Katzenberger contributed to this report.

The Trump administration is once again trying to limit who can become an American, with a pair of executive orders issued this week that attempt to place restrictions on birthright citizenship and on foreigners who give birth in the U.S.

A Supreme Court decision in June struck down a previous attempt at restricting birthright citizenship, but Thursday’s orders were made with “adjustments” keeping the decision in mind, President Donald Trump said.

Still, some of the restrictions announced by the White House are expected to face legal challenges.

The 14th Amendment, which makes a citizen of anyone born in the country, and two subsequent Supreme Court decisions interpreting it provide guidelines that already exclude certain births from receiving the citizenship benefit.

Trump’s new attempt to restrict birthright citizenship even after the Supreme Court loss highlights the administration’s drive to limit who can become an American.

Birthright citizenship is guaranteed under current law for anyone who is born on U.S. soil, with a few exceptions.

The executive order released Thursday was narrower in scope than the previous one shot down by the Supreme Court and appeared to focus on restricting automatic citizenship to specific categories of people, including children born to adults with connections to foreign embassies or organizations as well as anyone considered an “alien enemy” of the United States.

U.S. immigration law says babies born to a “foreign diplomatic officer accredited to the United States” are not entitled to birthright citizenship under the Constitution, including ambassadors, ministers, chargés d’affaires, counselors, secretaries and attachés of embassies and legations, and members of the Delegation of the Commission of the European Communities.

sources.body: <p>La idea de agosto como un mes desierto de actividad parlamentaria parece cosa del pasado. La agitada vida política española —y mundial—, así como <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-08-10/un-gobierno-en-emergencia-permanente.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-08-10/un-gobierno-en-emergencia-permanente.html">la sucesión de emergencias que el Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez</a> viene encadenando desde la pandemia, han transformado el escasísimo programa estival de las Cortes en uno más nutrido. Este verano, la agenda no para a cuenta del estallido de la inédita crisis de Ceuta, de la que el PP responsabiliza a La Moncloa, y encamina al Senado y al Ejecutivo hacia un choque institucional entre ambos. De un lado, el PP, con mayoría absoluta en la Cámara alta, donde ha registrado las solicitudes de comparecencia de los ministros de Interior, Defensa y Exteriores. En la otra esquina, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, Margarita Robles y José Manuel Albares, que no responderán a la cita para evitar “duplicidad” alegando que ya darán explicaciones por propia iniciativa a final de mes en el Congreso. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-08-11/el-gobierno-y-el-senado-se-encaminan-hacia-un-choque-institucional-por-las-comparecencias-sobre-la-crisis-de-ceuta.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

Once días más tarde de la entrada masiva de personas migrantes a Ceuta, la situación continúa preocupando a las autoridades locales. Según su presidente, Juan Jesús Vivas , todavía permanecen entre 8.000 y 11.000 personas en situación irregular en la ciudad autónoma. Para analizar la situación, Vivas se ha reunido este lunes con el ministro de Política Territorial, Ángel Víctor Torres, a quien le ha trasladado su petición para que el Gobierno active un plan que permita a Ceuta "volver a la normalidad".

Según Vivas, el Ejecutivo central debería habilitar con carácter "urgente" un nuevo centro de internamiento para personas extranjeras, para que "estén confinados y tengan restringida la libertad de movimiento hasta que se culminen los expedientes de expulsión ". El presidente ceutí ha remarcado que esto debe ser "una cuestión del Estado" y que el Gobierno local "colaborará".

La petición de este nuevo centro debería acabar con la sensación de "inseguridad" que, según Vivas, se vive en Ceuta. " Son miles de personas deambulando por la calles, miles de personas sin techo, generando inseguridad, siendo un alto riesgo para la convivencia ", ha dicho a los medios tras la reunión con el ministro Torres.

"Si se logra de manera ugente, se conseguirá que las necesidades vitales las tengan cubiertas y que no estén en nuestras calles y que se pueda tramitar con mayor facilidad los expedientes de expulsión", ha insistido Vivas. También ha dicho que se necesitan más medios para facilitar estos expedientes, con refuerzos de personal de extranjería, fiscalía, justícia y policía .

Las palabras de Vivas llegan más de una semana después de que miles de personas cruzaran la fronteras los días 30 y 31 de julio. Muchos de ellos hacen su vida en espacios como la playa del Trampolín , ya que los centros de acogida se encuentran saturados. Algunas de las imágenes que se pueden observar estos días son de tiendas de campaña en el litoral, así como cabañas hechas con todo tipo de materiales.

El Gobierno admite escuchar las peticiones de Ceuta y centra su actuación en intentar avanzar en la filiación de los menores no acompañados y trabajar en el reagrupamiento familiar para que vuelvan a su país de origen. Así lo ha manifestado el ministro de Política Territorial, Ángel Víctor Torres , tras reunirse este lunes con Vivas en Ceuta.

Según él, el reagrupamiento debe ser "la prioridad", aunque ha reconocido que "no es un proceso fácil" porque depende en parte de la colaboración que quiera prestar el Reino de Marruecos. El ministro Torres también ha anunciado que este martes se desplazará a la ciudad el ministro de Exteriores, José Manuel Albares , y que la ministra de Defensa, Margarita Robles, lo hará "posteriormente".

La reunión de este lunes se ha producido un día después de que miles de ceutíes se hayan manifestado para reclamar una solución a la crisis migratoria que allí se vive. Más de 10.000 personas según la organización y algo más de 5.000 según la Policía Nacional, han querido mostrar unidad y pedir una respuesta efectiva por parte de las autoridades.

La primera ministra d'Itàlia, Giorgia Meloni , ha aconseguit el suport de la de Dinamarca, Mette Frederiksen , en la seva ofensiva per frenar la immigració a la Unió Europea .

Totes dues han fet públic aquest dilluns un comunicat conjunt penjat a les seves xarxes socials en què diuen que els preocupa l'" impacte negatiu " de la immigració i que estan d'acord en com evitar-lo.

També que coincideixen en el rebuig a la " immigració descontrolada" i en la promoció d'" una política d'immigració rigorosa " als seus respectius països:

Ningú pot negar que la immigració il·legal té un impacte negatiu en les nostres societats: augment de les taxes de criminalitat, més pressió sobre els serveis públics i erosió de la confiança pública.

Relacionen així directament la immigració amb la delinqüència, però sense aportar cap dada o estadística que ho corrobori, i quan les dades oficials de Frontex mostren que les entrades irregulars per les fronteres de la UE han baixat gairebé a la meitat en l'últim any.

Totes dues admeten que provenen de "posicions polítiques molt diferents", l' extrema dreta en el cas de Meloni, la socialdemocràcia en el de Frederiksen, però que malgrat això estan d'acord en política migratòria .

Se centren en els aspectes negatius de la immigració, sobretot en els " delictes violents " que asseguren que cometen els " migrants il·legals ", especialment "el tràfic de drogues" i la "violència sexual".

I aposten per les mateixes solucions: augmentar les expulsions dels delinqüents, però també "establir centres de repatriació en tercers països" i "altres solucions innovadores fora d'Europa".

Afirmen que els mouen els mateixos motius: "Garantir més seguretat i protecció per a les nostres comunitats", i també defensar i protegir " el patrimoni cultural cristià d'Europa".

En aquest sentit, diuen que no n'hi ha prou amb les expulsions i els centres de repatriació, sinó que també cal que el respecte a les lleis vagi acompanyat del " respecte als valors europeus ":

Això s'aplica tant als immigrants irregulars com als milions de ciutadans estrangers que resideixen legalment en els nostres països i a tot Europa.

Frederiksen ha donat aquest suport explícit a Meloni en la seva pugna amb Espanya per la crisi migratòria de Ceuta de fa deu dies, quan desenes de milers de persones van travessar la frontera irregularment.

La primera ministra italiana va decidir llavors suspendre l'entrada sense restriccions de ciutadans no comunitaris procedents d'Espanya, congelant de facto el Tractat de Schengen , que ho permet.

Meloni va afirmar que era una mesura extraordinària i temporal , però el govern espanyol va qualificar la mesura de " desproporcionada " i va respondre dies després establint controls fronterers als viatgers procedents d'Itàlia .

Meloni va aconseguir l'octubre del 2024 que deu països de la UE , entre els quals Dinamarca, donessin suport a la iniciativa de buscar " fórmules innovadores contra la migració il·legal ".

El juny d'aquest any, i quan ja era un grup de dinou països els que ho reclamaven, la UE va avalar la creació dels anomenats " hubs de retorn ", és a dir, centres de deportació de migrants irregulars situats a fora del territori comunitari.

sources.body: <p>El Gobierno salió este lunes al paso para atajar el revuelo causado ante las informaciones sobre las alertas de Defensa y del CNI <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-08-10/la-instalacion-de-una-planta-china-junto-a-la-base-naval-de-ferrol-enciende-las-alertas-en-defensa-y-el-cni.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-08-10/la-instalacion-de-una-planta-china-junto-a-la-base-naval-de-ferrol-enciende-las-alertas-en-defensa-y-el-cni.html">por el proyecto para instalar una factoría china en Ferrol</a>, la ciudad que alberga una de las mayores instalaciones de la Armada española y el astillero militar de Navantia. El Ejecutivo dejó claro que mantiene su apoyo a la fábrica planeada por el mayor productor chino de coches eléctricos, SAIC Motor, con una inversión prevista de 200 millones de euros y la consiguiente creación de un millar de puestos de trabajo <a href="https://elpais.com/economia/2026-06-16/saic-el-mana-del-coche-chino-que-promete-hacer-florecer-una-comarca-de-ferrol.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/economia/2026-06-16/saic-el-mana-del-coche-chino-que-promete-hacer-florecer-una-comarca-de-ferrol.html">en una comarca que arrastra una histórica depresión económica</a>. El Gabinete de Pedro Sánchez quiso enviar un mensaje tranquilizador ante la preocupación suscitada tanto en las autoridades gallegas —la Xunta del PP la considera una inversión estratégica— como en Sumar, el socio minoritario del Gobierno. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-08-10/el-gobierno-mantiene-su-apoyo-a-la-fabrica-china-en-ferrol-pese-a-las-alertas-de-defensa.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>
sources.headline: El Gobierno mantiene su apoyo a la fábrica china en Ferrol pese a las alertas de Defensa

sources.body:
El Ministerio de Defensa ha reconocido que existe "preocupación" por la cercanía de la planta china que quiere abrir SAIC Motor en Ferrol con el arsenal militar y el astillero de Navantia que allí se encuentra. Fuentes de Defensa confirman a RTVE que la preocupación viene por "el riesgo de espionaje" .

La "preocupación" que expresa el ministerio de Defensa llega tras advertir la posibilidad de que esta futura factoría de coches se pueda llegar a utilizar como plataforma para espiar las instalaciones del arsenal militar y del astillero Navantia. Solo les separaría unos cinco kilómetros en línea recta .

Sin embargo, la postura del departamento que dirige Margarita Robles contrasta con la del ministro de Transformación Digital y Función Pública, Óscar López , que ha defendido la instalación de esta planta china y que ha dado por hecho que se garantizará la seguridad nacional.

"Es una inversión importante para nuestro país", ha sostenido el ministro, al mismo tiempo que ha hablado de "normalidad" porque se tienen en cuenta "todos los elementos" antes de acceder a una inversión como esta. También ha precisado que se pueden poner "condiciones" para garantizar todos los elementos de seguridad.

"Como otras inversiones de este calado, con toda normalidad se analizan todos los elementos económicos, industriales ,de empleo y de seguridad nacional (...). Se están teniendo en cuenta todos los elementos, también los de seguridad nacional ", ha sostenido López este lunes, durante un acto en Madrid. "Estas inversiones son analizadas y puede pasar que haya una serie de recomendaciones, desde el punto de vista económico o de la seguridad, que se atienden y hacen viable la operación", ha añadido.

La empresa ha ahondado también en esta línea, asegurando que el proyecto, que considera "de suma importancia para la zona y para el país", respetará "íntegramente" la seguridad nacional, pese a que entiende que "se evalúen todos los factores relevantes" para su puesta en marcha definitiva.

La alerta manifestada desde Defensa no ha sido bien recibida por la Xunta de Galicia , que lleva meses trabajando para atraer esta inversión a Ferrol. Su presidente, Alfonso Rueda, ha asegurado que la situación es "difícil de entender", ya que se trata de un expediente trabajado con el Gobierno de España.

"Conocemos perfectamente todo su contenido y las circunstancias que inciden, y ahora es sorprendente y difícil de entender que un departamento del Gobierno central haga estos pronunciamientos cuando en ningún momento se habló de falta de seguridad ni riesgo militar", ha apuntado Rueda en una atención a los medios de comunicación este lunes.

Por ello, Rueda ha responsabilizado al Ejecutivo de que sea capaz de "compatibilizar la seguridad nacional con la oportunidad fantástica, histórica, que se le presenta a Galicia con esta oportunidad industrial". "Es un poco sorprendente que, en estos momentos, el mayor riesgo para la seguridad nacional venga de una fábrica de coches que se quiere instalar en Ferrol, me parece un poco chocante", ha asegurado.

Segons han avançat els diaris El País i El Mundo, el Ministeri de Defensa i els serveis d'intel·ligència alerten, en un seguit d'informes, del risc d'espionatge . I recorden que la nova planta del grup xinès SAIC, fabricant de la coneguda marca MG, obrirà a tocar de l'arsenal militar de Ferrol i les drassanes de Navantia, on es treballa amb sistemes militars dels Estats Units.

Però el govern espanyol defensa aquesta operació estratègica , que tindrà una inversió inicial de 200 milions d'euros i crearà 1.000 llocs de treball.

Aquest dilluns, el ministre per a la Transformació Digital i de la Funció Pública, Óscar López , s'ha mostrat convençut que la instal·lació de la fàbrica es farà amb total garantia per a la seguretat de l'Estat .

Estic convençut que serà compatible garantir el desenvolupament industrial, la creació de llocs de feina i la seguretat nacional.

López ha assegurat que es fan informes d'aquest tipus sobre qualsevol gran inversió, i ha insistit que la instal·lació d'aquesta fàbrica la primera de la marca a Europa és "important" per a Espanya.

Tot i això, i davant les recances de l'exèrcit, ha advertit que es poden posar "condicions" a SAIC abans que s'instal·lin a Galícia.

Des de la Xunta també consideren que aquesta inversió és estratègica, i lamenten que ara es posi en entredit l'emplaçament de la fàbrica.

Així ho ha expressat el president gallec, Alfonso Rueda , que ha dit que li sembla "sorprenent i difícil d'entendre" que des d'un departament del govern central "es facin aquests pronunciaments, quan en cap moment es va parlar de falta de seguretat ni de risc militar".

Elías Bendodo, coordinador general del partit, ha dit que el govern espanyol no els ha facilitat "cap informació al respecte" , i que si hi ha cap risc per a la seguretat de l'Estat els correspon a ells fer-ho públic.

stories.headline: Catalunya prepares transport, safety and viewing plans for the August 12 total solar eclipse

sources.body:
El 12 d'agost Catalunya viurà l' eclipsi solar total , un esdeveniment excepcional per al qual s'espera un volum molt elevat de desplaçaments . El fenomen serà visible a tot el territori, entre les 19.30 i les 21.00, en funció de la ubicació, però només serà total al sud del país – especialment les comarques del Camp de Tarragona, les Terres de l'Ebre i zones de les Terres de Ponent –. La fase de totalitat durarà entre 28 segons i 1 minut i 32 segons.

Davant d'aquesta situació, el govern desplegarà un dispositiu especial de mobilitat, seguretat i salut pública, que ha presentat aquest matí. El Pla de Protecció Civil de Catalunya (Procicat) s'iniciarà l'11 d'agost i finalitzarà quan acabin les activitats i mobilitats previstes.

La consellera d'Interior i Seguretat Pública, Núria Parlon , i la consellera de Recerca i Universitats, Núria Montserrat , han explicat les principals mesures del pla, en què participaran efectius dels Mossos d'Esquadra, Protecció Civil, els Agents Rurals, el Servei Català de Trànsit, el Sistema d'Emergències Mèdiques i representants dels diferents municipis.

"Estem davant un esdeveniment únic que té un elevat valor científic i volem aproximar-lo a la ciutadania. Es preveu que hi hagi molta expectació entre la població autòctona i els visitants i, per aquest motiu, hem articulat un dispositiu perquè sigui un esdeveniment d'èxit", ha assenyalat la consellera d'Interior, Núria Parlon, que ha comparat l'eclipsi amb la magnitud d'esdeveniments recents com la visita del papa Lleó XIV o el Tour de França.

En aquest sentit, la consellera Núria Montserrat ha destacat la iniciativa " Catalunya mira al cel ", amb la celebració de nombroses activitats de divulgació científica vinculades a l'eclipsi per apropar la ciència a la ciutadania.

Tot i que no hi ha una previsió exacta de la mobilitat que pot generar l'eclipsi solar total del dia 12 d'agost, el govern ha dissenyat un dispositiu especial perquè l'esdeveniment es pugui desenvolupar amb la màxima seguretat.

Per aquest motiu, hi ha 18 punts oficials d'observació segura, ubicats en divuit municipis , que poden acollir fins a 50.000 persones i amb capacitat per a 20.000 vehicles.

Aquests punts s'han establert tenint en compte que compleixen els " criteris de seguretat i capacitat adients", segons el govern. S'han considerat espais amplis, amb bones condicions d'accés, mobilitat i visibilitat. Aquests punts estaran preparats per a grans afluències de públic i comptaran amb la presència d'efectius del pla.

Aproximadament uns 60 municipis han informat el govern d'algun tipus d'activitat relacionada amb l'eclipsi, element que també pot afavorir el repartiment de les persones que vagin a veure l'eclipsi més enllà dels punts d'observació oficials.

Fins a 700 efectius dels Mossos d'Esquadra vetllaran per la mobilitat a les carreteres del Camp de Tarragona, les Terres de l'Ebre i les Terres de Ponent, les principals zones d'observació.

En aquest sentit, Trànsit recomana fer servir vies d'alta capacitat alternatives a l'AP-7 , que serà l'eix principal de mobilitat i on es restringirà la circulació als camions en sentit sud entre les 14 i les 24 hores entre Martorell i Ulldecona. Tampoc podran circular per l'N-340 des de Vilafranca del Penedès fins a Ulldecona.

sources.body:
Ivan Sánchez Mota, aficionado a la astrofotografía de Toledo, ayer con su equipo en uno de los puntos de observación preparados en Prades para seguir el eclipse 

“Espero este eclipse desde hace dos años, quiero vivirlo con mi familia”, cuenta, nervioso, Iván Sánchez Mota, de 19 años, que viajó el domingo con padres y hermana desde Quintanar de la Orden (Toledo) hasta Prades, en Tarragona. En el maletero, un enorme telescopio (1,5 metros) y un equipo semiprofesional (casi 3.000 euros) a pesar de ser un aficionado a la astrofotografía. Ni de broma iba a desplazarse hoy o el día del eclipse y jugársela a encontrar las carreteras colapsadas.

Como Iván, ya han adelantado sus desplazamientos a los lugares de observación una parte de los 446.700 turistas adicionales motivados por el fenómeno astronómico, según los cálculos del Ministerio de Economía, Comercio y Empresa. La mayoría españoles (282.700); el resto, del extranjero.

“Llevo noches durmiendo mal, estoy muy nerviosa, es mi primera vez, es un privilegio que sea cerca de casa”, explica Noemí León, desplazada desde Girona hasta Prades, pequeño pueblo del interior de Tarragona, a 1.000 metros de altitud, famoso por la calidad de su cielo estrellado. La lista de visitantes es larguísima, como las procedencias: Estados Unidos, Japón, Brasil u Holanda, como Nicolás Capati, de origen argentino, “entusiasmado de ver tanta gente reunida por esta movida”.

Vivirlo en comunidad es otro de los factores que explica que el festival organizado por el Parc Astronòmic Muntanyes de Prades, de cuatro días, con un sinfín de actividades divulgativas, haya sido un éxito rotundo, con más de un millar de inscritos. El Ayuntamiento de Prades (650 vecinos que cada verano se multiplican por diez) ha dispuesto cerca de 1.000 plazas extras de aparcamiento antes de entrar al pueblo y estima que podrían reunirse unas 10.000 personas el día del eclipse.

“Nos hace mucha ilusión ser un referente a nivel mundial, viene gente de todo el mundo”, destaca Lídia Bargas, su alcaldesa, que admite que una de las grandes dificultades es que no saben cuántas personas llegarán.

La mayoría de los visitantes que se desplazarán hasta las comarcas de Tarragona y Terres de l’Ebre, atraídos por la totalidad, vienen de otros puntos de Catalunya, muchos del área metropolitana de Barcelona. “Espero que nos impresione mucho”, destaca Núria Carulla junto a sus dos hijas y una amiga. “Intentaré vivirlo con todos los sentidos, quiero hacerlo en comunidad, con mucha gente”, añade Karina Ibraev, su hija.

El mismo estudio del Ministerio de Economía estima que podrían registrarse aumentos del tráfico de entre un 30% y el 100% hacia la franja de totalidad del eclipse, lo que supone entre 400.000 y 1,5 millones de desplazamientos adicionales.

La coincidencia del eclipse con agosto, uno de los meses con mayor movilidad del año porque gran parte de la población está de vacaciones, hace prever una afluencia especial de vehículos hacia las zonas de observación. Un 8,4% de las personas con planes para ver el eclipse pretenden desplazarse a otra provincia distinta de la de su residencia.
